title: Untangle lifetime reservations and rewrite grace-period manager for GPU nodes
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: The capacity planner and node lifecycle code currently coordinate GPU lifetime reservations (short-lived lease records used for burst/buffer capacity) through a mix of in-memory caches, ad-hoc tombstone markers, and several edge-case reconciliation paths. Over time this led to high GC-like churn during large scale reconciles, sporadic double-allocations, and frequent eviction flaps when nodes transition between PROVISIONING -> READY -> DRAINING. The grace-period manager that determines when to mark a node as evictable is tightly coupled to the reservation cache and uses several implicit assumptions about event ordering.

Scope: This ticket refactors the lifetime reservation representation and replaces the current grace-period manager with a small, event-driven, idempotent controller. Work includes: (1) define a compact on-disk reservation table (versioned rows) that is the canonical source-of-truth, (2) migrate existing in-memory cache usage to read-through with short-lived local caches, (3) implement a proof-of-concept compact/compaction pass to remove stale tombstones, (4) rewrite the grace-period manager to subscribe to node state transitions and reservation lifecycle events, and (5) implement a safe migration path and rollout policy that can be rolled back without losing reservations.

Why now: Customers are hitting bursty provisioning workloads with Dedicated pools; these workloads exposed race conditions under scale and increase tail latency for allocation calls. Reducing reconcile work and stabilizing eviction behavior will lower allocation tail latency, reduce failed allocations (~P99 allocation errors), and decrease operator toil during upgrades.

Non-goals: This ticket does not change allocator scheduling policy (packing/anti-affinity) or implement new autoscaling strategies. It focuses on data model+controller hygiene and removing sources of churn.
acceptance_criteria: Reservation canonical table implemented and persisted to etcd with versioning and schema v1
Existing allocation paths read from the new table via read-through cache with TTL <= 250ms
Compaction pass removes >95% of tombstones seen in synthetic scale tests (100k reservations) without data loss
Grace-period manager rewritten to be event-driven and demonstrates idempotent behavior under duplicate events
No increase in allocation error rate during staged rollout (baseline ±2%) and P99 allocation latency improves by at least 25% in perf harness
Rollback is possible via feature-flag toggle within 30 minutes with zero reservation loss for active allocations
steps: Design: finalize reservation table schema and event contracts (confluence: /drive/gpu-fleet/reservation-schema-v1)
Implement: reservation-store component (read/write/compact) with unit + integration tests
Implement: read-through cache wrapper used by capacity planner and allocator paths
Implement: event-driven grace-period manager that subscribes to node/reservation events
Migration: build migration job that converts in-memory tombstones into versioned rows with changelog
Testing: run scale perf harness (k=100k reservations) and node churn scenarios; collect metrics
Rollout: gated rollout using feature-flag and canary pool, monitor metrics and rollback if regressions
Cleanup: remove legacy tombstone code paths and old cache primitives after 2 successful cycles
notes: Trade-offs: moving canonical reservation state into etcd increases write amplification; mitigated by batching commits and compacting tombstones periodically
Alternative considered: a sharded in-RAM coordinator with persistent snapshots — rejected due to operational complexity for Private deployments
Design review feedback (2026-02-20 by Priya Singh): ensure compaction does not block regular reconciles and expose compaction metrics
Security note: reservation table contains no customer PII; still follow KMS access patterns for etcd backups
Performance target: reduce average reconcile CPU for capacity-planner by 40% under burst load
rollout_plan: Stage 1 (Canary): enable feature-flag on 1 small Dedicated pool (10 nodes) for 48h
Stage 2 (Limited): enable on 10% of Dedicated capacity for 72h and run synthetic churn tests
Stage 3 (Gradual): ramp to 50% over 7 days while monitoring metrics and incidents
Full: enable globally after 2 successful cycles and cleanup legacy code after 14 days
